questions.q: What is the difference between JDK, JRE and JVM?
questions.a: The JVM executes bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the core class libraries needed to run a program. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, javadoc and the debugger.
questions.explain: You install a JDK to compile; an end user only needs a JRE. Modern JDKs bundle a JRE image, which is why the distinction is mostly about tooling.
questions.example: javac Hello.java produces Hello.class, which java Hello runs on the JVM.
questions.followUp: Is the JVM platform-dependent or platform-independent?
questions.tip: Say 'write once, run anywhere' only about bytecode — the JVM itself is platform-specific.

questions.q: Why is the main method declared public static void main(String[] args)?
questions.a: public so the launcher can call it, static so no instance is needed, void because it returns nothing, and String[] args carries command-line arguments.
questions.explain: Each keyword is enforced by the launcher's lookup. A missing static throws NoSuchMethodError at startup, not a compile error.
questions.example: java Main one two gives args = [one, two].
questions.followUp: What happens if main is not static?
questions.tip: Mention that since Java 21 a launch protocol can also run an instance main, but the classic signature is what interviews expect.

questions.q: What are the eight primitive types and their sizes?
questions.a: byte 8, short 16, int 32, long 64, float 32, double 64, char 16 (unsigned), boolean (JVM-dependent, typically one byte).
questions.explain: Primitives hold values directly on the stack or inside objects; wrappers hold references to heap objects. Sizes are fixed by the spec except boolean.
questions.example: int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE; // 2147483647
questions.followUp: Why is char unsigned?
questions.tip: Remember that String is not a primitive — it is a final class.

questions.q: What is the difference between == and equals for strings?
questions.a: == compares references (same object), equals compares content. Use equals, or equalsIgnoreCase, for text.
questions.explain: String literals are interned, so == may accidentally work for literals and then fail for new String or runtime-built values.
questions.example: new String("java") == "java" is false; equals is true.
questions.followUp: What does intern() do?
questions.tip: Mention the trap: == works in a demo and fails with user input.

questions.q: Why is String immutable?
questions.a: Its character data cannot change after construction, which makes it thread-safe, safely shareable, usable as a HashMap key, and lets the JVM cache the hash and intern literals.
questions.explain: Every 'modifying' method returns a new String. Immutability also protects security-sensitive values such as class names and file paths.
questions.example: s.toUpperCase() returns a new object; s is unchanged.
questions.followUp: How do you build large strings efficiently?
questions.tip: Connect immutability to safe caching and thread safety, not just 'it cannot change'.
questions.code:
String s = "java";
String upper = s.toUpperCase(); // s is still "java"

questions.q: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?
questions.a: String is immutable, StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronized, StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized (legacy). Use StringBuilder in single-threaded code.
questions.explain: Concatenating in a loop with + creates a new String each iteration, which is O(n^2). StringBuilder appends into one growable buffer.
questions.example: for (...) sb.append(word).append(' ');
questions.followUp: Does the compiler optimise string concatenation?
questions.tip: Note that javac uses invokedynamic/StringConcatFactory for a single + expression, but loops still need StringBuilder.

questions.q: What does final mean in its three positions?
questions.a: final variable: cannot be reassigned; final method: cannot be overridden; final class: cannot be extended. For objects, final freezes the reference, not the object's state.
questions.explain: final fields also get safe-publication guarantees when set in a constructor, which matters in concurrent code.
questions.example: final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); list.add("x"); // legal
questions.followUp: Can a final field be assigned twice?
questions.tip: Say explicitly that a final reference to a mutable object can still mutate.
questions.code:
final int limit = 10;
// limit = 20; // compile error

questions.q: What does static mean?
questions.a: static members belong to the class, not to instances: one copy shared by all objects, callable without an instance, initialised when the class is loaded.
questions.explain: Static methods cannot use this or instance fields directly. Static state is global mutable state and is a common source of bugs and test leakage.
questions.example: Math.max is static; a Counter's value field should not be.
questions.followUp: What is a static initializer?
questions.tip: Mention the memory-model angle: static initialisation happens under class-initialisation locking.

questions.q: Explain private, package-private, protected and public.
questions.a: private: class only. package-private (no modifier): same package. protected: same package plus subclasses. public: everywhere.
questions.explain: protected is the one people get wrong: a subclass in another package can access inherited protected members through its own reference, not through an arbitrary parent reference.
questions.example: Fields private, behaviour public, extension points protected.
questions.followUp: Why prefer private fields with getters?
questions.tip: Say 'encapsulation' and give the real rule for protected across packages.

questions.q: What is a constructor and can it be overloaded?
questions.a: A constructor initialises a new object, has the class name and no return type, and can be overloaded. If none is declared, the compiler adds a no-arg constructor.
questions.explain: Declaring any constructor removes the implicit no-arg one, which is why adding a parameterised constructor breaks code that relied on new Foo().
questions.example: new Student("Aman", 80) selects the matching constructor.
questions.followUp: What is constructor chaining with this(...)?
questions.tip: Mention that this(...) and super(...) must be the first statement.

questions.q: What is the this keyword?
questions.a: this is a reference to the current object. It disambiguates fields from parameters, passes the object to other methods, and chains constructors.
questions.explain: In a constructor, this(...) calls another constructor of the same class and must be the first statement.
questions.example: this.name = name; resolves the shadowed field.
questions.followUp: Can this be used in a static method?
questions.tip: Static methods have no this — that is the follow-up answer.

questions.q: Array vs ArrayList?
questions.a: Arrays are fixed-size, can hold primitives, and are faster with less overhead. ArrayList is resizable, holds objects only, and offers convenient methods.
questions.explain: ArrayList is backed by an array that grows (typically 1.5x). Autoboxing means an ArrayList<Integer> stores Integer objects, not ints.
questions.example: List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(); list.add(1);
questions.followUp: When would you use an array in production?
questions.tip: Mention primitive boxing cost and the fixed-size advantage.
questions.code:
int[] a = new int[3];
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

questions.q: How does a HashMap work at a high level?
questions.a: It hashes the key, finds a bucket, and stores entries there. Collisions are chained in a linked list that converts to a red-black tree when a bucket grows large. Lookup is O(1) on average.
questions.explain: Keys need consistent equals and hashCode. Immutable keys are safest because a mutated key can no longer be found.
questions.example: map.put("pen", 5); map.get("pen") returns 5.
questions.followUp: What happens when the map exceeds its load factor?
questions.tip: Say 'average O(1), worst O(log n) with treeified buckets'.
questions.code:
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
stock.merge("pen", 1, Integer::sum);

questions.q: Explain the four pillars of OOP with Java examples.
questions.a: Encapsulation hides state behind methods; inheritance reuses a parent type; polymorphism lets one reference call type-specific behaviour; abstraction exposes a contract without the implementation.
questions.explain: A Shape interface with area() is abstraction and polymorphism; private fields with methods are encapsulation; Manager extends Employee is inheritance.
questions.example: List<Shape> shapes; for (Shape s : shapes) total += s.area();
questions.followUp: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
questions.tip: Give one concrete code shape per pillar rather than definitions alone.
questions.code: interface Shape { double area(); }

questions.q: Abstract class vs interface — when do you use each?
questions.a: An abstract class shares state and partial implementation with a single inheritance chain. An interface defines a capability and supports multiple implementation.
questions.explain: Use an abstract class when subclasses share fields and template logic; use an interface for roles such as Comparable or Runnable, and for API boundaries.
questions.example: Abstract Repository<T> with shared storage; interface PaymentGateway for multiple providers.
questions.followUp: Can an interface have default and static methods?
questions.tip: Mention that a class can implement many interfaces but extend one class.
questions.code:
abstract class Animal { abstract String sound(); }
interface Pet { default String greet() { return "hi"; } }

questions.q: Overloading vs overriding?
questions.a: Overloading: same name, different parameter lists, resolved at compile time. Overriding: subclass replaces an inherited method with the same signature, resolved at runtime.
questions.explain: Overriding requires an accessible, non-final, non-static method and a covariant or identical return type. @Override turns a signature mistake into a compile error.
questions.example: print(int) and print(String) overload; Dog.speak() overrides Animal.speak().
questions.followUp: Can you overload a method that differs only in return type?
questions.tip: Say 'static binding vs dynamic dispatch'.
questions.code:
class Animal { String speak() { return "..."; } }
class Dog extends Animal { @Override String speak() { return "woof"; } }

questions.q: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?
questions.a: Checked exceptions extend Exception (not RuntimeException) and must be caught or declared. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and signal programming errors.
questions.explain: IOException is checked because the caller can recover; NullPointerException is unchecked because the fix is code, not a catch block.
questions.example: Files.readString throws IOException; int x = null throws NPE.
questions.followUp: When would you create a custom exception?
questions.tip: Do not say 'checked are better' — explain recoverability.

questions.q: What is try-with-resources and why use it?
questions.a: It closes every resource declared in the try header automatically, in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown. The resource must implement AutoCloseable.
questions.explain: It also suppresses secondary close exceptions onto the primary one, avoiding the classic finally-block bug where close() hides the real failure.
questions.example: try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { ... }
questions.followUp: What happens if both the body and close() throw?
questions.tip: Mention suppression via getSuppressed().

questions.q: What is the equals/hashCode contract?
questions.a: If two objects are equal, they must return the same hashCode. equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and return false for null.
questions.explain: Hash collections find the bucket by hashCode, then confirm with equals. Breaking the contract makes equal objects unfindable or duplicated.
questions.example: A HashSet of two equal Students has size 1 only if both methods are overridden.
questions.followUp: How do records help?
questions.tip: Say 'broken contract = duplicate keys in HashMap'.
questions.code: @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(name); }

questions.q: ArrayList vs LinkedList?
questions.a: ArrayList is an array-backed list with O(1) random access and amortised O(1) append. LinkedList is a doubly linked list with O(1) insert/remove at the ends but O(n) access.
questions.explain: In practice ArrayList wins for most workloads because of cache locality; ArrayDeque is the better queue/stack choice than LinkedList.
questions.example: list.get(500_000) is instant for ArrayList and slow for LinkedList.
questions.followUp: Which deque should you use for a queue?
questions.tip: Mention memory overhead per node and cache locality.
questions.code:
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

questions.q: What happens inside HashMap when it grows?
questions.a: When size exceeds capacity × load factor (default 0.75), the table doubles and entries are redistributed. A bucket with 8+ entries and capacity 64+ treeifies into a red-black tree.
questions.explain: Resizing is O(n) but amortised. Treeification protects against hash-collision attacks and pathological keys.
questions.example: new HashMap<>(16, 0.75f) resizes at the 13th entry.
questions.followUp: Why must keys be immutable?
questions.tip: Know the numbers 0.75, 8 and 64.

questions.q: Comparable vs Comparator?
questions.a: Comparable defines the natural order inside the class via compareTo. Comparator is an external, composable ordering that can be created per use case.
questions.explain: Use Comparator when you need several orderings or cannot modify the class. thenComparing builds multi-key sorts, and reversed flips one key.
questions.example: Comparator.comparingInt(Student::score).reversed().thenComparing(Student::name).
questions.followUp: Why should you avoid a-b in a comparator?
questions.tip: Mention Integer.compare to avoid overflow.
questions.code: students.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::score).reversed());

questions.q: How do you design an immutable class?
questions.a: Make the class final, all fields private final, provide no setters, defensively copy mutable inputs and outputs, and do not leak this during construction.
questions.explain: Immutability gives thread safety, safe sharing and reliable hash keys. Records give a concise immutable carrier.
questions.example: List.copyOf(toppings) in the constructor prevents external mutation.
questions.followUp: Are records always immutable?
questions.tip: Note that a record with a mutable array component is still mutable.

questions.q: What is type erasure?
questions.a: Generic type parameters exist only at compile time; the compiler erases them to their bounds (usually Object) and inserts casts. At runtime there is no List<String> versus List<Integer>.
questions.explain: That is why you cannot do new T(), instanceof List<String>, or overload on generic type alone. Arrays are covariant and reified, generics are invariant and erased.
questions.example: List<String> and List<Integer> both become List at runtime.
questions.followUp: How do you create a generic array safely?
questions.tip: Say 'erasure explains every restriction interviewers ask about'.
questions.code:
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
// names.getClass() == ArrayList.class

questions.q: What are wildcards ? extends T and ? super T for?
questions.a: ? extends T reads T values (covariant), ? super T writes T values (contravariant). Use PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
questions.explain: List<? extends Number> can be read as Number but not added to; List<? super Integer> can be added to but only read as Object.
questions.example: void sum(List<? extends Number> nums) accepts List<Integer> and List<Double>.
questions.followUp: Why can't you add to a ? extends list?
questions.tip: Use the PECS phrase and one example each.

questions.q: What are the pitfalls of autoboxing?
questions.a: Boxing allocates objects, unboxing a null throws NullPointerException, and == on wrappers compares references. Cached values (-128..127) can make == appear to work.
questions.explain: Use equals for wrapper comparison and prefer primitives in hot loops. Map.get returning null is the classic unboxing NPE.
questions.example: Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true, but 128 gives false.
questions.followUp: Why does Integer cache small values?
questions.tip: Mention the cache range and the NPE risk.
questions.code:
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
int v = map.getOrDefault("x", 0);

questions.q: What is the string pool and what does intern() do?
questions.a: The pool stores one copy of each string literal. intern() returns the pooled instance for an equal value, so references can be compared and memory shared.
questions.explain: Literals are interned automatically; runtime-built strings are not, unless you call intern(). Interning arbitrary user input can grow the pool without bound.
questions.example: "java".intern() == "java" is true.
questions.followUp: Why is interning risky for untrusted input?
questions.tip: Connect it to == behaviour in demos.

questions.q: What are default and static methods in interfaces?
questions.a: default methods provide an implementation that implementing classes inherit and may override; static methods belong to the interface and are called on its name.
questions.explain: Default methods enabled adding stream() and forEach() to existing collections without breaking implementors. Diamond conflicts must be resolved by overriding.
questions.example: interface Greeter { default String greet() { return "hi"; } }
questions.followUp: What happens when two interfaces provide the same default method?
questions.tip: Mention binary compatibility as the motivation.

questions.q: Describe the JVM memory areas and garbage collection.
questions.a: Heap holds objects (young and old generations), stack holds frames and local variables per thread, metaspace holds class metadata, plus PC registers and native stacks. GC reclaims unreachable heap objects.
questions.explain: Minor GC collects the young generation with copying collectors; major/old collections are more expensive. G1 is the default collector on modern JDKs and targets a pause-time goal.
questions.example: -Xms2g -Xmx2g fixes the heap; -XX:+UseG1GC selects G1.
questions.followUp: What is a memory leak in a garbage-collected language?
questions.tip: Say 'reachable, not referenced-count' — leaks are unintended strong references.

questions.q: volatile vs synchronized?
questions.a: volatile guarantees visibility and ordering for a single variable but not atomicity. synchronized provides mutual exclusion plus visibility for a block or method.
questions.explain: count++ on a volatile int still loses updates because read-modify-write is not atomic. AtomicInteger or synchronized fixes it.
questions.example: volatile boolean running = true; is a correct stop flag.
questions.followUp: What does happens-before mean?
questions.tip: Give the stop-flag example and the counter counter-example.
questions.code:
private volatile boolean running = true;

public void stop() { running = false; }

questions.q: What causes deadlock and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: Two or more threads wait forever for locks held by each other, forming a circular wait. Prevent it with a global lock order, lock timeouts (tryLock), fewer locks, or lock-free structures.
questions.explain: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Breaking any one condition prevents it; consistent ordering breaks circular wait.
questions.example: Thread 1 locks A then B; thread 2 locks B then A.
questions.followUp: How do you diagnose a deadlock in production?
questions.tip: Mention jstack and thread dumps showing 'found one Java-level deadlock'.
questions.code:
synchronized (A) { synchronized (B) { } }
// every thread uses the same A-then-B order

questions.q: How do you size a thread pool?
questions.a: Start from CPU count. CPU-bound work: about N or N+1 threads. I/O-bound work: higher, based on N × (1 + wait/compute), or use virtual threads in Java 21.
questions.explain: Too few threads underutilises the machine; too many cause context-switch and memory overhead. Bound the queue and choose a rejection policy.
questions.example: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()).
questions.followUp: When are virtual threads a better fit?
questions.tip: Mention bounded queues and backpressure.
questions.code:
int n = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n);

questions.q: What is CompletableFuture used for?
questions.a: It composes asynchronous work: supplyAsync, thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine, exception handling with exceptionally/handle, and timeouts.
questions.explain: It turns nested callbacks into a pipeline and lets independent stages run concurrently. Always handle failures, otherwise they surface only at join/get.
questions.example: supplyAsync(() -> price(id)).thenApply(p -> p * 1.18).join()
questions.followUp: thenApply vs thenCompose?
questions.tip: thenCompose flattens a future-returning function; thenApply maps a value.

questions.q: Why are streams lazy, and what does that buy you?
questions.a: Intermediate operations only describe work; a terminal operation drives it. Laziness enables fusion, short-circuiting (findFirst, anyMatch) and avoiding unnecessary computation.
questions.explain: A stream is consumed once. Side effects in intermediate operations are discouraged because they may not run or may run in a different order.
questions.example: stream.filter(...).findFirst() stops after the first match.
questions.followUp: Why is peek() not for business logic?
questions.tip: Say 'no terminal operation, no work'.
questions.code:
Optional<Integer> first = IntStream.range(1, 100)
    .filter(i -> i % 7 == 0)
    .boxed()
    .findFirst();

questions.q: When does parallelStream hurt?
questions.a: With small data, I/O, ordered dependencies, or shared mutable state. It can be slower and can produce wrong results through data races.
questions.explain: Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool; blocking work there starves other tasks. Measure before parallelising, and prefer reductions over mutation.
questions.example: Adding to an ArrayList inside parallel forEach loses elements.
questions.followUp: Which collector is safe in parallel?
questions.tip: Mention the common pool and blocking I/O risk.

questions.q: What is reflection and when is it appropriate?
questions.a: Reflection inspects and invokes classes, methods and fields at runtime. Frameworks (Spring, JUnit, Jackson) need it; application code usually should not.
questions.explain: It bypasses compile-time checks, is slower, and can break encapsulation. Prefer interfaces or code generation for normal design.
questions.example: Main.class.getAnnotation(Info.class).author()
questions.followUp: What is a dynamic proxy?
questions.tip: Name a real framework use case, not just 'it is powerful'.
questions.code:
Method m = String.class.getMethod("length");
Object len = m.invoke("java"); // 4

questions.q: What are records and sealed classes for?
questions.a: Records are concise immutable data carriers with generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Sealed types restrict which classes may extend or implement them.
questions.explain: Together they model closed data hierarchies, enabling exhaustive pattern matching switch without a default.
questions.example: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
questions.followUp: Can a record have validation?
questions.tip: Mention compact constructors for validation.

questions.q: Explain the factory and strategy patterns in Java.
questions.a: Factory centralises object creation behind a method or class. Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind an interface so the choice happens at runtime.
questions.explain: Both replace conditionals at call sites with polymorphism. A switch expression in the factory is acceptable because creation is the one place that must know concrete types.
questions.example: Shape create(String type); Comparator as a strategy passed to sort.
questions.followUp: How does dependency injection relate to factory?
questions.tip: Give a code-level example of each, not just definitions.

questions.q: Strong, soft, weak and phantom references?
questions.a: Strong references prevent collection. Soft references are cleared under memory pressure (caches). Weak references are cleared at the next GC (canonical maps). Phantom references are for post-mortem cleanup.
questions.explain: Reference queues let you learn when a reference was cleared. WeakHashMap keys are weak, so entries disappear when the key is unreachable.
questions.example: Caches often use SoftReference or a bounded cache library instead.
questions.followUp: Why can a WeakHashMap entry vanish unexpectedly?
questions.tip: Connect weak references to ThreadLocal and listener leaks.
questions.code: WeakReference<byte[]> ref = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1024]);

questions.q: What is the happens-before relationship?
questions.a: It is the JMM guarantee that memory writes by one action are visible to another. Program order, monitor unlock→lock, volatile write→read, thread start and join all create happens-before edges.
questions.explain: Without an edge, a thread may see stale or reordered values even on real hardware. Synchronization is about visibility as much as mutual exclusion.
questions.example: Writing a field before starting a thread is visible to that thread.
questions.followUp: Does final field publication need synchronization?
questions.tip: Mention safe publication and final field semantics.

questions.q: What are the default values of fields and local variables?
questions.a: Fields get type defaults: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for references. Local variables get no default and must be initialised before use.
questions.explain: The compiler rejects reading an uninitialised local. Fields are zeroed when the object is allocated, which is why null fields surprise people later.
questions.example: int field; // 0 inside a class; int local; // compile error if read
questions.followUp: Why does Java not default-initialise locals?
questions.tip: Contrast fields and locals explicitly — that is the point of the question.
questions.code: class Box { int value; } // new Box().value == 0

questions.q: if/else vs switch: when do you choose which?
questions.a: Use if for ranges and complex boolean conditions; use switch for a fixed set of discrete values. A switch expression returns a value and is exhaustive for enums and sealed types.
questions.explain: Arrow cases avoid accidental fall-through. Modern switch also supports patterns, guards and null handling.
questions.example: String size = switch (code) { case 1 -> "small"; default -> "other"; };
questions.followUp: What is fall-through and how do you avoid it?
questions.tip: Mention switch expressions, not just the classic statement.

questions.q: for vs while vs do-while?
questions.a: for when the iteration count is known and the counter is local to the loop; while when the condition drives repetition; do-while when the body must run at least once.
questions.explain: The enhanced for iterates arrays and Iterables without index bookkeeping and cannot easily remove elements.
questions.example: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) is the standard counted loop.
questions.followUp: When is a do-while a genuinely better choice?
questions.tip: Give a real do-while case such as a menu that must render once.
questions.code:
int i = 0;
while (i < 3) { System.out.println(i); i++; }

questions.q: break vs continue vs return?
questions.a: break exits the nearest loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration; return leaves the whole method.
questions.explain: In nested loops break only exits the inner loop. Use a labelled break or extract a method with return to exit both.
questions.example: for (...) { if (skip) continue; if (done) break; }
questions.followUp: How do you break out of two nested loops cleanly?
questions.tip: Mention labelled break but recommend extracting a method.

questions.q: What does a method signature include?
questions.a: Name plus parameter types (and order). Return type and parameter names are not part of the signature, so you cannot overload on return type alone.
questions.explain: The compiler resolves overloads using the static types of the arguments, including widening, boxing and varargs in a defined order.
questions.example: sum(int, int) and sum(long, long) are different signatures.
questions.followUp: Can two methods differ only by throws clause?
questions.tip: Say clearly that return type is not part of the signature.
questions.code:
static int sum(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
static long sum(long a, long b) { return a + b; }

questions.q: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.a: Always pass-by-value: the value of the variable is copied. For objects, the copied value is the reference, so the callee can mutate the object but cannot reassign the caller's variable.
questions.explain: Reassigning the parameter inside the method has no effect outside. Mutating the referenced object is visible to the caller.
questions.example: void add(List<String> l) { l.add("x"); } changes the caller's list.
questions.followUp: How do you make an object argument effectively immutable?
questions.tip: Say 'pass-by-value of the reference' — that is the precise answer.
questions.code:
static void replace(List<String> list) { list = new ArrayList<>(); }
// caller's list is unchanged

questions.q: Which String methods should you know cold?
questions.a: length, charAt, substring(begin,end), indexOf, contains, startsWith, endsWith, split, replace, trim/strip, toUpperCase, equals, compareTo, and formatted.
questions.explain: substring's end is exclusive, split takes a regex, and trim removes only ASCII whitespace while strip handles Unicode.
questions.example: "java".substring(1, 3) returns "av".
questions.followUp: How do you check for a blank string?
questions.tip: Mention isBlank() for whitespace-only strings.
questions.code:
String s = "  java  ";
System.out.println(s.strip()); // java

questions.q: How do you copy and compare arrays?
questions.a: Copy with Arrays.copyOf, clone or System.arraycopy; compare content with Arrays.equals (deepEquals for nested arrays). == compares references.
questions.explain: Arrays.toString gives readable output for logs and failing tests. Sorting uses Arrays.sort, or parallelSort for large arrays.
questions.example: Arrays.equals(new int[]{1}, new int[]{1}) is true.
questions.followUp: Does clone() deep-copy an object array?
questions.tip: Note that clone is shallow for object elements.

questions.q: What is null and what is NullPointerException?
questions.a: null means a reference points to no object. Dereferencing it (field access, method call, unboxing, array access) throws NullPointerException.
questions.explain: Defensive checks, Optional for return values, and Objects.requireNonNull at boundaries reduce NPEs. Annotations such as @Nullable help tooling.
questions.example: String s = null; s.length() throws NPE.
questions.followUp: What does Optional actually solve?
questions.tip: Say Optional is for return types, not fields.
questions.code:
String s = null;
System.out.println(s == null ? "missing" : s.length());

questions.q: What are packages and imports for?
questions.a: Packages namespace classes and control access; imports bring simple names into scope. java.lang is imported automatically.
questions.explain: The package must match the directory layout for build tools. A fully qualified name avoids ambiguity when two packages contain the same class.
questions.example: import java.util.List; then write List<String>.
questions.followUp: What is the default package and why avoid it?
questions.tip: Mention that imports do not load classes, they only resolve names.
questions.code:
package com.brocode.app;

import java.util.List;

questions.q: Compile-time error vs runtime exception vs error?
questions.a: Compile-time errors stop javac (syntax, type mismatch). Runtime exceptions are thrown during execution. Errors (such as OutOfMemoryError) signal serious JVM problems that applications usually should not catch.
questions.explain: A program that compiles can still fail logically; tests and assertions catch that class of bug.
questions.example: Missing semicolon: compile error. Array index out of bounds: runtime exception.
questions.followUp: Should you catch Throwable?
questions.tip: Do not catch Error in normal application code.

questions.q: Why write Javadoc and how is it different from comments?
questions.a: Javadoc is structured documentation attached to public API and rendered by the javadoc tool. Ordinary comments explain implementation and are not extracted.
questions.explain: Write Javadoc for contracts: what a method does, parameters, return value and thrown exceptions — not for restating the code.
questions.example: /** Returns the sum. @param a first addend @return a + b */
questions.followUp: What Javadoc tags matter most?
questions.tip: Say that outdated Javadoc is worse than none.
questions.code:
/**
 * Adds two numbers.
 * @param a first addend
 * @param b second addend
 * @return the sum
 */
static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

questions.q: Stack vs heap in Java?
questions.a: Each thread has a stack of frames holding locals, parameters and partial results; objects and arrays live on the shared heap. References live on the stack (or inside other heap objects).
questions.explain: Stack memory is reclaimed automatically when a method returns; heap memory is reclaimed by the garbage collector. Deep recursion overflows the stack.
questions.example: A local int is on the stack; new int[1000] allocates on the heap.
questions.followUp: Why does recursion cause StackOverflowError?
questions.tip: Say objects are on the heap but references can be anywhere.

questions.q: Explain the order of initialisation when an object is created.
questions.a: Static initialisers and static fields run once when the class is first used; then instance field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks run in textual order, then the constructor body.
questions.explain: The superclass constructor runs before the subclass's fields are initialised, so calling an overridable method from a constructor can observe uninitialised subclass state.
questions.example: A constructor calling a method that reads a not-yet-assigned subclass field sees 0 or null.
questions.followUp: Why should constructors avoid calling overridable methods?
questions.tip: Mention the superclass-first rule and the overridable-method trap.

questions.q: What are exception best practices?
questions.a: Catch only what you can handle, catch specific types, never swallow silently, wrap with context and preserve the cause, and do not use exceptions for normal control flow.
questions.explain: Logging and rethrowing causes duplicate noise; pick one boundary that logs. Clean up with try-with-resources rather than finally.
questions.example: throw new IllegalStateException("account " + id + " is closed", e);
questions.followUp: What does it mean to preserve the cause?
questions.tip: Mention the cause chain in the constructor.

questions.q: How does finally interact with return and exceptions?
questions.a: finally always runs (except on System.exit or JVM crash). A return in finally overrides a pending return and discards exceptions, which is why returning from finally is banned in most style guides.
questions.explain: An exception thrown in finally replaces the original one; try-with-resources instead suppresses close failures onto the primary exception.
questions.example: try { return 5; } finally { return 0; } returns 0.
questions.followUp: When is finally still necessary?
questions.tip: Say 'never return from finally' as a rule.

questions.q: List.of vs Arrays.asList vs Collections.unmodifiableList?
questions.a: List.of is immutable, rejects nulls, and is a compact value-based list. Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view backed by the array (set allowed, add/remove not). unmodifiableList is a read-only view over a mutable list.
questions.explain: A view still reflects changes to the backing collection; List.of is truly independent and immutable.
questions.example: Arrays.asList(1,2).add(3) throws UnsupportedOperationException.
questions.followUp: How do you get a mutable copy?
questions.tip: new ArrayList<>(List.of(...)) is the usual mutable copy.

questions.q: entrySet vs keySet vs values?
questions.a: keySet iterates keys, values iterates values, entrySet iterates key-value pairs and is the efficient choice when you need both.
questions.explain: Iterating keySet and calling get(key) for each entry does a second lookup per element and can be wrong if the map changes.
questions.example: for (Map.Entry<K,V> e : map.entrySet()) use both e.getKey() and e.getValue().
questions.followUp: Can you remove entries through entrySet?
questions.tip: Mention entrySet().removeIf for filtering.
questions.code:
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : map.entrySet())
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue());

questions.q: How does a HashSet work?
questions.a: It is backed by a HashMap where elements are keys and a shared placeholder is the value. add computes hashCode, finds the bucket, then checks equals.
questions.explain: Duplicate detection depends on both methods. Mutable elements are dangerous because their hash can change after insertion.
questions.example: Adding the same String twice keeps one element and returns false the second time.
questions.followUp: What is the average complexity of contains?
questions.tip: Say 'HashSet is a HashMap with dummy values'.

questions.q: HashMap vs TreeMap vs LinkedHashMap?
questions.a: HashMap is unordered and fastest on average; TreeMap keeps keys sorted with O(log n) operations and needs Comparable or a Comparator; LinkedHashMap keeps insertion or access order.
questions.explain: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true is the basis of a simple LRU cache via removeEldestEntry.
questions.example: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) for LRU.
questions.followUp: How would you build an LRU cache with the standard library?
questions.tip: Give the accessOrder + removeEldestEntry recipe.

questions.q: Deque vs Stack?
questions.a: Stack is a legacy synchronized class; Deque (usually ArrayDeque) is the modern choice for stack and queue behaviour, offering push/pop and addLast/pollFirst.
questions.explain: ArrayDeque is faster and not synchronized, and it rejects nulls. Use java.util.concurrent structures when threads share it.
questions.example: Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); stack.push(1);
questions.followUp: Which deque operation is FIFO?
questions.tip: Say 'do not use java.util.Stack in new code'.

questions.q: When should you use var?
questions.a: Use var when the type is obvious from the initialiser and the variable is local. Avoid it when it hides the type, in field declarations (not allowed), or when the inferred type is an implementation detail.
questions.explain: var is compile-time inference, not dynamic typing. The variable still has a fixed static type.
questions.example: var users = new HashMap<String, List<User>>(); is readable; var x = get(); is not.
questions.followUp: Can var be used in a lambda parameter?
questions.tip: Emphasise readability over brevity.
questions.code:
var counts = new HashMap<String, Integer>();
for (var entry : counts.entrySet()) { }

questions.q: What is a switch expression and what rules apply?
questions.a: It returns a value, uses arrow labels, requires exhaustiveness (default or all enum/sealed cases), and every branch must produce a compatible value. yield returns from a block.
questions.explain: Exhaustiveness is checked for enums and sealed hierarchies, so adding a case later becomes a compile error instead of a silent fallthrough bug.
questions.example: int days = switch (month) { case 2 -> 28; case 4, 6, 9, 11 -> 30; default -> 31; };
questions.followUp: How does pattern matching in switch help?
questions.tip: Mention that no fall-through is possible with arrows.

questions.q: What are text blocks and when do you use them?
questions.a: Text blocks are multi-line string literals delimited by three double quotes. They preserve newlines, strip incidental indentation and are ideal for SQL, JSON and HTML.
questions.explain: Use \s to keep a trailing space and \ to join lines without a newline. Formatted fills placeholders.
questions.example: String json = """\n{"id": 1}\n""";
questions.followUp: How does indentation stripping work?
questions.tip: Mention that the closing delimiter position sets the common indentation.
questions.code:
String sql = """
    SELECT id, name
    FROM students
    WHERE marks > ?
    """;

questions.q: What are Optional best practices?
questions.a: Return Optional from methods that may have no result; use map/flatMap/orElse/orElseGet/ifPresent; never call get() without a check; do not use Optional for fields, parameters or collections.
questions.explain: Optional is a return-type tool that makes absence explicit in the API. An empty Optional is not null, and Optional.of(null) throws.
questions.example: find(id).map(User::name).orElse("unknown")
questions.followUp: orElse vs orElseGet?
questions.tip: orElseGet avoids building a default that is not needed.
questions.code: String name = find(id).map(User::name).orElse("unknown");

questions.q: map vs flatMap?
questions.a: map transforms one element into one element; flatMap transforms each element into a stream and flattens the results into one stream.
questions.explain: Use flatMap for nested collections or Optional chains, such as a list of orders each with many items.
questions.example: orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.items().stream()).count()
questions.followUp: How do you flatten a List<List<Integer>>?
questions.tip: Say 'map one-to-one, flatMap one-to-many'.

questions.q: collect vs reduce?
questions.a: reduce combines elements into a single value with a binary operator; collect gathers into a container using a Collector, which supports mutable accumulation, grouping and downstream collectors.
questions.explain: Prefer collect for strings and collections, reduce for numeric aggregation. A reduce function must be associative for parallel streams.
questions.example: sum() is a specialised reduce; Collectors.joining() builds a string.
questions.followUp: Why must reduce be associative?
questions.tip: Mention that String concatenation in reduce is O(n^2).
questions.code:
int sum = List.of(1, 2, 3).stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);
String csv = List.of("a", "b").stream().collect(Collectors.joining(","));

questions.q: How does class loading work?
questions.a: Loading finds the bytecode, linking verifies and prepares it and resolves symbolic references, and initialisation runs static initialisers. Parent-first delegation asks the bootstrap and platform loaders before the application loader.
questions.explain: Class initialisation is lazy and thread-safe, triggered by new, static access or reflection. ClassLoader leaks keep whole applications alive in containers.
questions.example: Class.forName("com.example.Main") triggers loading and initialisation.
questions.followUp: What causes a ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError?
questions.tip: Distinguish missing at lookup vs failed earlier initialisation.
questions.code: Class<?> type = Class.forName("java.lang.String");

questions.q: What does the JIT compiler do?
questions.a: It profiles hot methods and compiles bytecode to native code, applying inlining, escape analysis and loop optimisations. Cold code stays interpreted; deoptimisation rolls back speculative assumptions.
questions.explain: Tiered compilation starts with C1 for fast warm-up and promotes hot code to C2. Microbenchmarks need warm-up and a harness such as JMH.
questions.example: A method called millions of times becomes a prime inlining candidate.
questions.followUp: Why are naive Java microbenchmarks misleading?
questions.tip: Mention warm-up, dead-code elimination and JMH.

questions.q: What are common GC tuning levers?
questions.a: Heap sizing (-Xms/-Xmx), collector choice (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah), pause-time goals (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis), and young-generation sizing. Start by measuring allocation rate and pause times.
questions.explain: Most throughput problems are allocation problems, not flag problems. Fix object churn first, then tune. Containers need -XX:MaxRAMPercentage rather than fixed sizes.
questions.example: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+UseG1GC in a container.
questions.followUp: When would you choose ZGC?
questions.tip: Say 'measure first, tune second'.
questions.code: java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 -jar app.jar

questions.q: What is ThreadLocal and when does it leak?
questions.a: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy of a value. In pooled threads the value survives between tasks unless remove() is called, which leaks memory and can leak data across users.
questions.explain: Libraries use ThreadLocal for request context, formatters and transactions. Always clear it in a finally block, or use scoped values where available.
questions.example: A DateFormat cached per thread is safe but must be removed in a pool.
questions.followUp: How do virtual threads change ThreadLocal usage?
questions.tip: Mention thread pools plus remove() in finally.

questions.q: synchronized vs ReentrantLock?
questions.a: Both provide mutual exclusion and visibility. ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible acquisition, fairness and multiple conditions; synchronized is simpler and released automatically.
questions.explain: Prefer synchronized unless you need those advanced features, since manual unlock in finally is easy to get wrong.
questions.example: if (lock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)) { try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
questions.followUp: What is lock fairness and what does it cost?
questions.tip: Say 'unlock must be in finally'.

questions.q: What is the ForkJoinPool and work stealing?
questions.a: A pool for recursive divide-and-conquer tasks. Idle workers steal subtasks from other workers' deques, keeping all cores busy. Parallel streams use the common pool.
questions.explain: Tasks should avoid blocking I/O, which stalls a worker and can starve the pool. Use managed blockers or a separate executor for blocking work.
questions.example: RecursiveTask<Integer> splitting an array range until a threshold.
questions.followUp: Why is blocking in a parallel stream dangerous?
questions.tip: Mention the common pool is shared JVM-wide.

questions.q: Race condition vs data race?
questions.a: A data race is unsynchronised concurrent access to the same memory with at least one write. A race condition is any timing-dependent correctness bug, which can occur even with proper locking (for example check-then-act).
questions.explain: You can have a race condition without a data race: two synchronized operations composed non-atomically still interleave incorrectly.
questions.example: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); is a race condition even on a synchronized map.
questions.followUp: How do you fix check-then-act?
questions.tip: Use computeIfAbsent for atomic check-and-put.
questions.code: map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value);

questions.q: What is safe publication?
questions.a: Making a fully constructed object visible to other threads with a happens-before edge: through a volatile field, a static initialiser, a final field, a concurrent collection, or lock handoff.
questions.explain: Without it another thread may see a partially constructed object with default field values, even though the constructor finished in program order.
questions.example: Storing the object in a volatile field or an AtomicReference publishes it safely.
questions.followUp: How do final fields help?
questions.tip: Connect it to the double-checked locking bug.
questions.code:
private volatile Config config;

void reload() { config = new Config(); }

questions.q: How do you write a custom Collector?
questions.a: Implement supplier (new container), accumulator (add one element), combiner (merge two containers for parallel) and finisher (optional final transform).
questions.explain: Collectors.of builds one; most needs are met by teeing, groupingBy with downstream collectors, or collectingAndThen.
questions.example: A collector that joins names into a sorted, comma-separated string.
questions.followUp: Why is the combiner required?
questions.tip: Explain the combiner's role in parallel processing.

questions.q: What are the risks of reflection and serialization?
questions.a: Reflection breaks encapsulation and compile-time checks and can fail under modules or renamed fields. Java serialization bypasses constructors, is fragile across versions and has a history of deserialization vulnerabilities.
questions.explain: Prefer explicit data binding (JSON) or serialization proxies. If you must deserialize untrusted data, use an allow-list filter.
questions.example: serialVersionUID mismatches break compatibility; gadget chains exploit readObject.
questions.followUp: What is a serialization filter?
questions.tip: Mention that records and explicit DTOs are safer than default serialization.

questions.q: What are virtual threads and when do they help?
questions.a: Virtual threads are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. They make blocking code scale to many concurrent tasks, especially I/O-bound servers.
questions.explain: They do not speed up CPU-bound work and can pin carrier threads inside synchronized blocks or native calls. Avoid pooling them; create one per task.
questions.example: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() handles thousands of blocking requests.
questions.followUp: What is pinning?
questions.tip: Say 'great for I/O, not for CPU, do not pool them'.

questions.q: How does pattern matching for switch work?
questions.a: Cases can test types with a binding variable, add guards with when, and destructure records. For sealed hierarchies the compiler enforces exhaustiveness, so no default is needed.
questions.explain: Order matters: more specific patterns must come first. Null must be handled explicitly with case null.
questions.example: case Circle(double r) -> Math.PI * r * r;
questions.followUp: Why is exhaustiveness valuable?
questions.tip: Mention that adding a new permitted subtype becomes a compile error at every switch.

questions.q: How do you find and fix a memory leak in a Java application?
questions.a: Reproduce the growth, capture heap dumps, compare dominator trees, and find objects that should have been collected but are still strongly reachable. Common causes are static caches, listeners never removed, ThreadLocal values and unbounded queues.
questions.explain: Tools: jcmd GC.heap_dump, Eclipse MAT, JFR allocation profiling. Fix by bounding caches, removing listeners, clearing ThreadLocals and closing resources.
questions.example: A static Map<Session, User> that never evicts grows until OutOfMemoryError.
questions.followUp: How do weak references help a cache?
questions.tip: Say 'reachable, not just allocated' — that is the definition of a leak here.
questions.code:
// leak: static map with no eviction
static final Map<String, byte[]> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
